section.title: Remember the LORD
section.sectionRationale: Moses turns from the severity of chapter 7 to the discipline of memory, retelling how God humbled and fed Israel in the wilderness to teach dependence on His word, and warning that the coming abundance of the land is a subtler danger than the hardship of the desert ever was.
section.thesis: Moses calls Israel to remember the whole of their wilderness journey, where God humbled and tested them with hunger and manna to teach that life comes from every word of His mouth, and warns that the abundance of the good land ahead poses the greater danger: forgetting the LORD who alone gives the power to gain wealth.
section.frameNote: Four movements: remembering the whole way, humbled and tested; the good land ahead; the warning against forgetting God in prosperity; and the reminder that it is the LORD who gives power to gain wealth.

units.label: Remember the whole way, humbled and tested
units.note: man does not live on bread alone

verses.text: You must carefully follow every commandment I am giving you today, so that you may live and multiply, and enter and possess the land that the LORD swore to give your fathers.

Remember that these forty years the LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might {{anah|humble}} you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments.

He humbled you, and in your hunger He gave you manna to eat, which neither you nor your fathers had known, so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.
Your clothing did not wear out and your feet did not swell during these forty years.
So know in your heart that just as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you.

units.label: The good land ahead
units.note: a land where you will lack nothing

verses.text: Therefore you shall keep the commandments of the LORD your God, walking in His ways and fearing Him.
For the LORD your God is bringing you into a good land, a land of brooks and fountains and springs that flow through the valleys and hills;
a land of wheat, barley, vines, fig trees, and pomegranates; a land of olive oil and honey;
a land where you will eat food without scarcity, where you will lack nothing; a land whose rocks are iron and whose hills are ready to be mined for copper.
When you eat and are satisfied, you are to bless the LORD your God for the good land that He has given you.
Be careful not to {{shakach|forget}} the LORD your God by failing to keep His commandments and ordinances and statutes, which I am giving you this day.
Otherwise, when you eat and are satisfied, when you build fine houses in which to dwell,
and when your herds and flocks grow large and your silver and gold increase and all that you have is multiplied,
then your heart will become proud, and you will forget the LORD your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
He led you through the vast and terrifying wilderness with its venomous snakes and scorpions, a thirsty and waterless land. He brought you water from the rock of flint.
He fed you in the wilderness with manna that your fathers had not known, in order to humble you and test you, so that in the end He might cause you to prosper.
You might say in your heart, “The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me.”

units.label: Remember who gives the power to gain wealth

verses.text: But remember that it is the LORD your God who gives you the {{koach|power}} to gain wealth, in order to confirm His covenant that He swore to your fathers even to this day.
If you ever forget the LORD your God and go after other gods to worship and bow down to them, I testify against you today that you will surely perish.
Like the nations that the LORD has destroyed before you, so you will perish if you do not obey the LORD your God.

anah.gloss: To humble, afflict, or bring low. Describes God's purposeful use of hardship, hunger in this case, not as cruelty but as discipline meant to reveal and reshape what is truly in a person's heart.

shakach.gloss: To forget, to cease remembering or acting on what one knows. In this chapter it describes the specific danger of prosperity: not doctrinal denial of God but a practical, functional amnesia that lets comfort crowd out active dependence on Him.

koach.gloss: Power, strength, ability. Used of the very capacity to work and produce wealth, undercutting any claim to self-made success by naming even one's productive strength itself as a gift from God.

basic.context: Moses looks back over forty years of wilderness wandering, explaining that God humbled Israel with hunger and then fed them with manna to teach dependence on His word, and now warns that the abundance of the good land ahead is actually a greater spiritual danger than the hardship of the wilderness ever was.
basic.hermeneutics: This is both memory and warning: a real history of hunger and provision that teaches a timeless truth, prosperity more easily produces forgetfulness of God than hardship does. Its call to actively remember God's provision applies directly to believers today, even though the specific wilderness details belong to Israel's unique history.
basic.originalLanguages: God used anah, humbling or affliction, purposefully, to test what was truly in Israel's heart. The chapter's central danger is that Israel would shakach, forget, God amid prosperity, wrongly crediting their own koach, strength or power, for wealth that was always a gift from Him.
basic.typology: Israel's wilderness testing over manna and bread anticipates and is directly recalled by Jesus' own wilderness temptation, where He is tested with hunger yet refuses to turn stones to bread, quoting this very chapter, Matthew 4:4, succeeding perfectly where Israel had so often failed.
basic.christ: When tempted to turn stones into bread after forty days of fasting, Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 8:3 directly, refusing to let physical need override trust in God's word, succeeding as the true and faithful Israel where the nation itself had so often failed in the wilderness.
basic.god: God disciplines His people as a father disciplines a son, using hardship purposefully rather than randomly, and He is also the generous giver of every good thing in the land ahead, including the very strength and ability by which people produce wealth.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 4:1-4 records Jesus quoting this chapter directly in His own wilderness temptation. Proverbs 30:8-9 echoes the same danger of both poverty and prosperity leading a heart away from God. 1 Timothy 6:17-19 warns the rich not to put their hope in wealth but in God.
basic.oneStory: This chapter names one of the deepest, most ordinary temptations of the faithful life: forgetting the God who provides once His provision becomes abundant and familiar. Christ succeeds perfectly where Israel failed, and His victory over the same temptation gives His people both an example and the grace to remember rightly.

context.literary:
Deuteronomy 8 is one of the most carefully shaped chapters in the book. Many readers see a concentric design. It opens and closes with life and death: follow the commands 'so that you may live,' verse 1, and 'you will surely perish' if you forget, verse 19. Inside that frame the wilderness is recalled twice, verses 2 to 6 and verses 14 to 16, each time with the same pair of verbs, 'humble you and test you,' verses 2 and 16, and each time with manna that their fathers had not known, verses 3 and 16. Between them the good land is described twice, first as promise, verses 7 to 10, then as possession, verses 12 and 13. At the centre stands verse 11: 'Be careful not to forget the LORD your God.'

The chapter is also built on paired sayings of the heart. God led Israel 'to know what was in your heart,' verse 2; Israel must 'know in your heart' that God disciplines them as sons, verse 5; the danger is that 'your heart will become proud,' verse 14, and that they will 'say in your heart,' 'The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me,' verse 17. The whole chapter is an examination of what the heart remembers and what it claims.

The phrase 'when you eat and are satisfied' appears in verse 10 and again in verse 12, first leading to blessing and then leading to pride. The same meal can end in thanksgiving or forgetting. The chapter ends by turning the previous chapter's language around: Israel will perish 'like the nations that the LORD has destroyed before you,' verse 20.

In the book's movement, chapter 8 follows the command to drive out the nations and precedes the reminder in chapter 9 that Israel is not righteous. Chapter 7 dealt with the danger of other gods; chapter 8 deals with the quieter danger of a self sufficient heart.
context.historical:
The generation Moses addressed had lived almost their whole lives on manna. Exodus 16:4 records God raining bread from heaven with the words, 'In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions,' and Exodus 16:15 explains the name: the people asked, 'What is it?' because they did not know. Deuteronomy 8:3 and 8:16 stress that neither this generation nor their fathers had known it. Their daily food was a daily miracle that could not be stored, Exodus 16:18, and it would stop once they ate the produce of the land, Joshua 5:12. Their clothes had not worn out and their feet had not swollen, verse 4, a detail repeated in Deuteronomy 29:5 and Nehemiah 9:21.

The wilderness of verse 15 is real terrain: the rocky deserts of Sinai and the Negev, where venomous snakes were a genuine danger, Numbers 21:6, and scorpions still live. The water 'from the rock of flint' recalls Exodus 17:6 and Numbers 20:11.

The land of verses 7 to 9 is described as a farmer would see it. Unlike Egypt, where fields were watered by irrigation, Canaan drank rain from heaven, Deuteronomy 11:10-11. Verse 8 lists seven products: wheat, barley, vines, figs, pomegranates, olive oil and honey, which Jewish tradition calls the seven species. The honey may include syrup made from fruit such as dates as well as bees' honey. Verse 9 mentions iron and copper; copper was mined in antiquity in the Arabah south of the Dead Sea, and iron ore was found in parts of the region.

The temptation of verse 17 had a religious form in Canaan. The peoples of the land credited rain and harvest to Baal. Hosea 2:8 later records exactly that failure: Israel did not acknowledge 'that it was I who gave her grain, new wine, and oil,' and used the silver and gold for Baal. Forgetting the LORD in prosperity easily became crediting another god. Verse 10, 'you are to bless the LORD your God for the good land,' became in Jewish practice the basis of the blessing said after meals.
context.canonical:
The chapter's warning echoes through Israel's later history. Hosea 13:6 summarises it almost word for word: 'When they had pasture, they became satisfied; when they were satisfied, their hearts became proud, and as a result they forgot Me.' The Song of Moses predicts the same, 'Jeshurun grew fat and kicked,' Deuteronomy 32:15, and Nehemiah 9:25-26 confesses that it happened. Proverbs 30:8-9 prays for neither poverty nor riches, lest 'I may have too much and deny You, saying, Who is the LORD?' Hezekiah's heart grew proud after God's favour, 2 Chronicles 32:25, and Nebuchadnezzar boasted of what he had built 'by the might of my power,' Daniel 4:30, words that sound like verse 17.

The psalms keep the wilderness memory alive. Psalm 78:24-25 calls manna 'grain from heaven' and 'the bread of angels'; Psalm 106:13-14 laments that 'they soon forgot His works' and tested God in the desert; Psalm 103:2 joins blessing and remembering, 'Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds,' the same pairing as Deuteronomy 8:10-11. Amos 8:11 threatens a famine 'of hearing the words of the LORD,' the hunger verse 3 warned of.

In the New Testament Jesus answers the tempter with verse 3, Matthew 4:4 and Luke 4:4, as the BSB footnote notes. In John 6 He calls Himself the true bread from heaven. Paul reads the wilderness in 1 Corinthians 10:1-12 as examples 'written down as warnings for us.' Hebrews 12:5-11 develops the fatherly discipline of verse 5 through Proverbs 3:11-12. Paul's question, 'What do you have that you did not receive?' 1 Corinthians 4:7, is verse 18 applied to spiritual gifts, and Jesus' parable of the rich fool, Luke 12:16-21, and His word to Laodicea, 'I am rich ... and need nothing,' Revelation 3:17, both describe the heart of verse 17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to read their past rightly. The forty years could be remembered as punishment, wasted time, or hardship to be forgotten. Moses reinterprets them as a school. God led them 'all the way,' verse 2, with purpose: to humble them, to test them, and to teach them. The hunger and the manna were a lesson that life depends on God's word, verse 3, and the unworn clothes were daily proof of His care, verse 4.

He also wanted them to read their future rightly. The land would be good in every way, and he describes it with obvious delight. But he wanted them to see that the gifts could become a trap. The chapter is not against prosperity; verse 10 commands them to eat, be satisfied and bless God. It is against a prosperity that forgets the Giver and credits the self, verse 17.

Finally, he wanted them to connect the two. The wilderness was preparation for the land. God humbled them 'so that in the end He might cause you to prosper,' verse 16. The lessons of hunger were meant to protect them in plenty. Moses' goal was a people who would remember in the land what they had learned in the desert, and who would give God thanks for every meal.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes events unique to Israel: forty years in the wilderness, manna, clothes that did not wear out, and entry into a particular land with its crops and metals. Believers today should not expect manna or identical provision. Nor should verse 18 be read as a promise that faithful believers will become wealthy. It concerns God's covenant with Israel in the land, 'in order to confirm His covenant that He swore to your fathers.'

The principles, however, are stated as general truths. 'Man does not live on bread alone,' verse 3, is quoted by Jesus as true of every person. The pattern of God using hardship to discipline His children is restated for the church in Hebrews 12:5-11. The command to bless God after eating, verse 10, lives on in the Christian practice of giving thanks. And the warnings against pride in wealth are repeated to Christian readers in 1 Timothy 6:17-19 and Luke 12:16-21. Paul's statement that these wilderness events 'were written down as warnings for us,' 1 Corinthians 10:11, gives the chapter's warnings direct force today.

debates.question: Was the wilderness hunger described in verses 2-3 primarily a punishment or a discipline?

views.label: Primarily fatherly discipline
views.case: Verse 5 explicitly frames it as a father disciplining a son, and verse 16 names the goal: 'so that in the end He might cause you to prosper.' The verbs humble, test and teach describe formation rather than penalty, and God's care is visible throughout, verses 4 and 15.

views.label: Discipline that includes consequence
views.case: The forty years were first a sentence for the unbelief at Kadesh-barnea, Numbers 14:29-34 and Deuteronomy 1:34-35. Some therefore read the wilderness as both a judgment on the older generation and a school for the younger one.

debates.bearing: The two are not opposed. The wilderness began as a consequence of unbelief, but for the generation that grew up in it God turned the consequence into training. Hebrews 12:10-11 describes the same result: discipline is painful but 'yields a harvest of righteousness and peace.'

debates.question: What does verse 2 mean when it says God tested Israel 'in order to know what was in your heart'?

views.label: Knowledge for Israel's sake
views.case: God already knows the heart, Psalm 139:1-4, so the testing was to reveal Israel to themselves. The verse speaks in human terms, as a father might say he is testing a child to see what he will do, when the point is the child's growth.

views.label: Knowledge through lived history
views.case: Others note that Scripture speaks of God coming to know through events, as in Genesis 22:12, 'now I know that you fear God.' On this view God's foreknowledge is not denied, but He also knows His people's obedience as something actually lived out in time.

debates.bearing: Both views affirm God's full knowledge and His purpose in testing. The practical point is that trials reveal what is in the heart, and that God uses them for good, as James 1:2-4 and 1 Peter 1:6-7 teach.

debates.question: Does verse 18 promise wealth to the faithful?

views.label: A covenant promise for Israel in the land
views.case: The verse ties the power to gain wealth to a specific purpose, 'to confirm His covenant that He swore to your fathers.' It belongs to the land promises of the Mosaic covenant, like the rain and harvest of Deuteronomy 11:13-15, and cannot be transferred as a promise of riches to individual believers.

views.label: A general truth about ability and gift
views.case: Others read the verse as stating a principle for everyone: whatever ability a person has to work and earn comes from God. It is not a promise that the faithful will be rich but a denial that anyone is self made, which 1 Corinthians 4:7 and James 1:17 also teach.

debates.bearing: The verse's force is not a guarantee of prosperity but a warning against pride. Its target is verse 17, the boast of self sufficiency. The New Testament warns that the love of money and the hope of riches are dangers, 1 Timothy 6:17, and Jesus says one cannot serve God and money, Matthew 6:24.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3 contains one of the best known sentences in Scripture, and the Hebrew is slightly different from the English. It says literally that man lives 'on everything that goes out from the mouth of the LORD,' kol motsa pi YHWH. The word 'word' is not in the Hebrew; the BSB, like most translations, supplies it. The Septuagint does the same, rendering it with 'every word,' and that is the form Jesus quotes in Matthew 4:4. The Hebrew phrase is broader: everything God speaks into being, including the manna itself, which came at His word, Exodus 16:4. Man lives not by bread alone, but by the God whose word creates the bread.

'Man' in verse 3 is ha-adam, the word for humanity in general, not a word for Israelites only. Moses draws a lesson from Israel's history that applies to every human being, which explains why Jesus can quote it as the answer of the true Man.

The verb 'test' in verses 2 and 16 is nasah, the same verb Deuteronomy 6:16 uses when it forbids Israel to test God. The contrast is deliberate. God may test His people, as He did with Abraham in Genesis 22:1 and with Israel at Marah, Exodus 15:25; His people may not test Him by demanding proof. Exodus 16:4 uses the same verb for manna: 'In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions.'

'Disciplines' in verse 5 is yasar, which means both to correct and to instruct. Its noun, musar, is the 'discipline' of Proverbs 3:11: 'do not reject the discipline of the LORD.' The word joins teaching and correction; Hebrews 12:5-11 draws out both, quoting Proverbs.

'You will lack nothing' in verse 9 uses chaser, to lack or be in want. Moses used it of the wilderness in Deuteronomy 2:7, 'you have lacked nothing,' and it is the verb of Psalm 23:1, 'I shall not want.' Israel had lacked nothing in the desert because of manna, and would lack nothing in the land because of harvest. The provider is the same in both places.

Two words in verse 15 recall specific stories. The 'venomous snakes' are nachash saraph, literally 'burning' or 'fiery' serpents, the creatures of Numbers 21:6-8, where Moses made a fiery serpent on a pole; Jesus uses that story of Himself in John 3:14. The 'rock of flint' is challamish, the word used in Psalm 114:8, 'the flint into a fountain of water.' The hardest rock gave water, a picture of provision from the least likely source.

Finally, the pairing of 'bless' and 'forget' in verses 10 and 11 is important. To bless the LORD is to acknowledge Him as the source of good; to forget is to fail to act on that knowledge. Psalm 103:2 joins the two in the same way, and so does the chapter: gratitude is the practical remedy for forgetfulness.

typology.type: Israel tested with hunger in the wilderness
typology.fulfillment: Israel, God's son, was led into the wilderness for forty years, humbled by hunger and tested to reveal the heart. Jesus, declared the beloved Son, is led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days and is hungry, Matthew 4:1-2. The tempter says, 'tell these stones to become bread,' and Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 8:3, Matthew 4:4. Where Israel grumbled and demanded food, the Son trusted His Father's word. The type is surpassed because Jesus does not only pass the test for Himself. As the faithful Son He becomes the representative of all who trust Him, 'tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15.

typology.type: Manna, bread not previously known, sustaining Israel
typology.fulfillment: Manna was bread from heaven, unknown before, given daily to keep Israel alive. In John 6 the crowd cites it, and Jesus answers that the Father gives 'the true bread from heaven,' John 6:32, and that He is that bread, John 6:35. The escalation is clear: 'Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died,' but whoever eats of the living bread 'will live forever,' John 6:49-51. At the Last Supper Jesus gives bread as His body, Luke 22:19. The type falls short because manna fed the body for a day; Christ gives eternal life. Revelation 2:17 promises the overcomer 'the hidden manna.'

typology.type: Water from the rock of flint (v.15)
typology.fulfillment: In the thirsty wilderness God gave water from the hardest rock, Exodus 17:6 and Psalm 114:8. Paul says Israel 'drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. Jesus invites the thirsty, 'let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37, promising streams of living water, the Spirit. The type points to a source of life that is found in Christ Himself. It is surpassed in the new creation, where the river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1.

Moses tells Israel that the wilderness was the discipline of a father for his son. Hebrews 12:5-11 takes up this picture through Proverbs 3:11-12 and applies it to believers: 'God is treating you as sons.' Hardship is not evidence of God's absence but of His fatherly care, aimed at sharing 'in His holiness.' The escalation comes in Christ, the Son who learned obedience through suffering, Hebrews 5:8, and through whom believers receive adoption as sons, Galatians 4:5. The type falls short because Israel often resisted the discipline; in Christ the Spirit makes children who receive it and grow.

study.christ:
The most direct link is the temptation of Jesus. Matthew tells it as a replay of Israel's wilderness. Jesus has just been declared God's beloved Son, Matthew 3:17, as Israel was called God's firstborn son, Exodus 4:22. He is led by the Spirit into the wilderness, as Israel was led by the pillar of cloud. He fasts forty days, matching Israel's forty years, and He is hungry, as Israel was hungry, Deuteronomy 8:3. The tempter's first words, 'If You are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread,' Matthew 4:3, press exactly the test of this chapter: will the son trust his father's word, or will he use his power to meet his own need?

Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 8:3: 'Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God,' Matthew 4:4. He does not argue or perform a miracle. He takes His place as a man, ha-adam, under God's word. The Son who could have made bread from stones chooses to live by His Father's voice, and in doing so succeeds where Israel failed. His whole ministry shows the same pattern. 'My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me,' He tells His disciples, John 4:34.

The chapter also leads to Christ through the manna. After Jesus fed the five thousand, the crowd pointed to Moses' manna and asked for a sign. Jesus answered that it was His Father who gave the bread from heaven, and that He Himself is 'the bread of life,' John 6:32-35. The manna of Deuteronomy 8 kept Israel alive for a day at a time, and the ones who ate it died. The bread Jesus gives is His own flesh, given 'for the life of the world,' John 6:51. At the Last Supper He took bread and said, 'This is My body, given for you,' Luke 22:19. The provision that humbled Israel in the desert points to the provision of Christ's own life.

The rock in verse 15 leads to Christ as well. Paul says the rock that gave water was Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4, and Jesus calls the thirsty to come to Him and drink, John 7:37. The same passage in Paul warns that the wilderness generation, though they ate and drank from Christ, fell, 1 Corinthians 10:5-12. The chapter's warning against forgetting applies to those who have received Christ's gifts.

Finally, the chapter's warning about prosperity finds its answer in Christ's example. Though He was rich, He became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9. He did not credit His life to His own strength, but lived in dependence on the Father. The proud heart of verse 17 is healed not by poverty but by union with the One who received everything from the Father and gave everything away.
study.god:
The chapter presents God as a Father who teaches through history. He 'led you all the way in the wilderness,' verse 2. Nothing in the forty years was accidental. The hunger, the manna, the unworn clothes and the protected feet were all part of His purpose. He is the kind of God who uses circumstances, even painful ones, to shape His children.

He humbles and He tests. These verbs can sound harsh, but the chapter explains them. He humbles 'so that you might understand' that life depends on His word, verse 3. He tests 'in order to know what was in your heart,' verse 2. And He does both 'so that in the end He might cause you to prosper,' verse 16. His severity serves His kindness. Verse 5 gives the governing image: 'just as a man disciplines his son.' Hebrews 12:10 draws the conclusion: 'God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His holiness.'

He provides abundantly and faithfully. In the wilderness He provided food no one had known, water from flint, and clothes that did not wear out. In the land He will provide brooks, springs, grain, fruit, oil, honey, iron and copper, verses 7 to 9. The chapter's catalogue of goods is a hymn to the generosity of God. The same God who sustains in scarcity gives in abundance. He is the source of both the manna and the harvest.

He is also the source of human capacity. Verse 18 says it is He 'who gives you the power to gain wealth.' Human skill, strength and effort are real, but they are His gifts. James 1:17 says every good and perfect gift comes from above. The chapter does not deny human work; it denies human self sufficiency.

He is faithful to His covenant. The purpose of His gifts is 'to confirm His covenant that He swore to your fathers,' verse 18. His provision is not random generosity but covenant faithfulness, the keeping of a promise made to Abraham.

He is jealous and just. The chapter ends with a sober warning: if Israel forgets Him and serves other gods, they will perish like the nations, verses 19 and 20. The same holiness that judged Canaan applies to Israel.

For worship, the chapter gives a simple and profound practice: 'When you eat and are satisfied, you are to bless the LORD your God,' verse 10. Every meal is an occasion to remember that life comes from God. Gratitude is the practical answer to pride, and remembering is the heart's defence against forgetting the God who gives.

crossReferences.note: Jesus, hungry after forty days, answers the tempter with Deuteronomy 8:3. He relives Israel's wilderness test as the true Son, choosing to live by God's word rather than use His power to satisfy His hunger, and so succeeds where Israel failed.

The original account of the manna. God rains bread from heaven, saying, 'In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions,' the people ask 'What is it?', and each gathers only what is needed. Deuteronomy 8 interprets this history as a lesson in dependence on God's word.

The crowd cites the manna, and Jesus answers that His Father gives the true bread from heaven and that He is the bread of life. Deuteronomy 8:3 and 8:16 stand behind the whole discourse, which moves from bread that sustains for a day to bread that gives eternal life.

Paul reads the wilderness events, including manna and water from the rock, as examples written for the church. He identifies the rock with Christ and warns that those who received these gifts still fell, echoing the warning of Deuteronomy 8:19-20.

Hebrews quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 and develops the image of Deuteronomy 8:5: God disciplines His children as a father does, for their good and so that they may share in His holiness. Hardship is reframed as evidence of sonship.

Hosea summarises the chapter's warning as history: when Israel had pasture they became satisfied, their hearts became proud, and they forgot the LORD. The very sequence Moses feared in Deuteronomy 8:12-14 came to pass.

The Song of Moses predicts that Jeshurun, a name for Israel, would grow fat and kick, abandoning the God who made him. It is the poetic counterpart to the warning of Deuteronomy 8, showing how abundance can lead to rebellion.

The wise man prays for neither poverty nor riches, lest in plenty he deny God and say, 'Who is the LORD?' It is a prayer shaped by the lesson of Deuteronomy 8, recognising the danger of abundance as well as need.

Israel failed to acknowledge that the LORD gave grain, new wine and oil, and used her silver and gold for Baal. This shows the form the forgetting of Deuteronomy 8:17 actually took in Canaan: crediting prosperity to another god.

Jesus' parable of the rich fool pictures the heart of Deuteronomy 8:17. The man plans for his abundance as if it were his own and ignores God, and God calls him a fool. Jesus warns against storing up treasure while not being rich toward God.

Paul tells the rich not to be conceited or to hope in uncertain wealth, but in God, 'who richly provides all things for us to enjoy.' It is Deuteronomy 8:18 applied to believers: enjoy the gifts, remember the Giver, and be generous.

Paul asks, 'What do you have that you did not receive?' and challenges the Corinthians' boasting. It is the logic of Deuteronomy 8:17-18 applied to spiritual gifts and status: nothing is self made, so pride is misplaced.

study.oneStory:
The chapter sits within the long story of humanity's dependence on God for life. In the garden, God gave every tree for food and one command to trust, Genesis 2:16-17. The first temptation was about food and the word of God, and humanity chose to trust its own judgment. Deuteronomy 8 returns to the same question: will God's people live by bread alone, or by His word? The wilderness was God's school in trust, a picture of the life for which humanity was made, receiving everything from His hand.

The chapter also sets up the story of Israel in the land. Moses foresaw both the gifts and the danger. The land was good, and Israel did eat and become satisfied. But as Hosea 13:6 records, their hearts became proud and they forgot the LORD. They credited Baal with the harvest, Hosea 2:8, and eventually went into exile, perishing 'like the nations' as verse 20 warned. The wilderness lesson had not been learned.

The story turns in Christ. He enters the wilderness as Israel's representative and answers the ancient temptation with this chapter's words, Matthew 4:4. He then offers Himself as the true bread from heaven, John 6:35, and the living water from the rock, John 7:37. Believers live by Him and are warned by Israel's story, 1 Corinthians 10:11-12. They are disciplined as sons, Hebrews 12:5-11, and learn contentment in both plenty and want, Philippians 4:11-13.

The story ends in a new creation where the wilderness and the land are both fulfilled. God's people will never again hunger or thirst, Revelation 7:16, for the Lamb will lead them to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17. The tree of life will bear fruit every month, Revelation 22:2, and the river of life will flow from the throne. There will be abundance without pride and satisfaction without forgetting. In that city every meal will be a blessing of the God who gives, and no heart will ever again say, 'The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me.'

sermon.title: Not by Bread Alone
sermon.why: Keller preaches directly through this chapter's warning about prosperity and forgetting God, drawing out how dependence on 'every word from the mouth of the LORD' is meant to shape practical, daily life after salvation, not only survival in the wilderness.

quiz.q: Why did God let Israel hunger and then feed them manna in the wilderness (v.3)?

options.text: To humble them and teach that man does not live on bread alone but on every word from the mouth of the LORD.
options.note: Verse 3 gives this exact reason, later quoted by Jesus in Matthew 4:4.

options.text: To punish them for a specific unnamed sin.
options.note: Verse 2 frames this as humbling and testing, not punishment for a specific named offense.

options.text: Because there was no other food available anywhere in the region.
options.note: The text presents the hunger and manna as purposeful teaching, not merely a logistical necessity.

options.text: No reason is given for the manna or the hunger.
options.note: Verse 3 gives an explicit, stated purpose.

quiz.q: How does Jesus use Deuteronomy 8:3 in the Gospels?

options.text: He quotes it directly when tempted by the devil to turn stones into bread, refusing to prioritize physical need over God's word.
options.note: Matthew 4:4 records Jesus quoting this verse word for word in His wilderness temptation.

options.text: He rejects it as no longer relevant.
options.note: Jesus affirms and applies it directly to His own temptation, the opposite of rejecting it.

options.text: He reinterprets it to mean bread is entirely unnecessary.
options.note: The verse and Jesus' use of it affirm bread's real necessity while placing greater weight on dependence on God's word.

options.text: Jesus never references this verse.
options.note: Matthew 4:4 records a direct quotation.

quiz.q: What specific danger does Moses warn will come with prosperity in the good land (vv.12-14)?

options.text: That when houses, herds, and wealth multiply, Israel's heart will become proud and forget the LORD who brought them out of Egypt.
options.note: Verses 12-14 describe this exact progression from abundance to pride to forgetting God.

options.text: That the land itself would become physically dangerous to live in.
options.note: The danger described is spiritual and internal, pride and forgetting, not a physical threat from the land.

options.text: That prosperity itself is inherently sinful and must be avoided.
options.note: The chapter presents prosperity as a genuine blessing from God, verses 7-10, while warning about its spiritual dangers.

options.text: No dangers of prosperity are mentioned in this chapter.
options.note: Verses 12-14 give a detailed, specific warning.

quiz.q: What does Moses say Israel must remember about the source of their ability to gain wealth (v.18)?

options.text: That it is the LORD who gives the power to gain wealth, in order to confirm His covenant.
options.note: Verse 18 states this directly, countering the claim in verse 17 that human strength alone produced the wealth.

options.text: That wealth comes entirely from human skill and effort alone.
options.note: Verse 17 presents this as the very claim Moses is correcting, not the truth he is affirming.

options.text: That wealth is randomly distributed with no cause at all.
options.note: Verse 18 names a specific source, the LORD, rather than randomness.

options.text: Nothing is said about the source of wealth.
options.note: Verse 18 makes an explicit statement about its source.

quiz.q: What warning does Moses give in verses 19-20 about forgetting the LORD and following other gods?

options.text: Israel would surely perish, just like the nations the LORD destroyed before them.
options.note: Verses 19-20 state this warning explicitly and starkly.

options.text: Israel would simply be fined a portion of their crops.
options.note: The stated consequence is far more severe, complete destruction, not a fine.

options.text: Nothing would happen once Israel was settled and secure in the land.
options.note: The text warns the opposite; settled security is precisely when this danger is greatest.

options.text: No warning at all is given in these verses.
options.note: Verses 19-20 give an explicit and severe warning.

questions: God let Israel go hungry before feeding them manna, to teach dependence on His word rather than bread alone. Where might God be humbling you right now to teach a deeper kind of dependence?

Jesus quoted this very verse when tempted in the wilderness, refusing to let a legitimate physical need override trust in God's word. Where are you tempted to meet a real need in a way that bypasses trust in God?

Moses warns that 'when you have eaten and are satisfied' is exactly when Israel's heart is most likely to grow proud. How has comfort or success in your own life quietly produced more self-reliance than gratitude?
Moses commands Israel to actively remember the LORD's provision, an intentional discipline, not an accident. What specific practices help you remember, rather than forget, what God has done for you?
The chapter ends with a stark warning that forgetting God leads to ruin. What is currently competing for the trust and attention that belongs only to God in your life right now?

translationNotes.note: This verse is quoted word for word by Jesus in Matthew 4:4 during His own wilderness temptation, making it one of the most directly fulfilled verses in Deuteronomy.
'Venomous snakes and scorpions' names real, concrete dangers of the Sinai wilderness, grounding the chapter's lesson about dependence in genuine historical hardship, not abstract metaphor.
'The power to gain wealth' identifies even human strength, skill, and ability itself as a gift from God, undercutting any claim to being entirely self-made.
